doc.title: Ramsey Lewis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Moving to Columbia: Clive Davis and George Butler
summary: He says he was with Chess then Columbia for about 19 years each, joined Columbia through Clive Davis around 1970-71, and praises George Butler.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah, we were there for – 19 years? I was at Columbia 19 years. I think I was with one of those companies 16 years and another company 19 years.

You started recording with them in ’56, and then you go on Columbia. I’ve seen two different accounts for Columbia. I saw the earliest discography said 1970, but then the Columbia reissue Best of Ramsey Lewis says it starts in ’72.
I think it was ’70, ’71.
That’s what the discography shows, right?
Yeah, ’70, ’71. So between those two companies, that was my major – because I think I’ve only been with, now, maybe five record companies in the 60 years that I’ve been in the business.
Columbia, I guess, that would have been the George Butler era? No . . . .
Yeah, yeah. I was there when George Butler was there.
Dr. George.
Dr. George, indeed.
Was he instrumental in bringing you in? Or was . . . ?
No. I got there before George Butler.
That’s right, in ’70.
Yeah, I was there. Clive Davis brought me in.
Still close? Or still . . . ?

No, no. I haven’t talked to Clive in years. I didn’t know him well then. Somebody suggested to him, this is a group that should be on our label. So, “Ramsey, this is Clive Davis.” From that point on, I think I might have seen him two or three times. Somebody else took over.
But with George, when George came on board, George Butler came on board . . .
He was the guy. He was the head of the jazz department. Very – George Butler was very easy to work with, very helpful, very well dressed, very well mannered. George was a nice guy.
I know his sister, Jackie Hairston, in Oakland.
In Oakland.
She’s very well mannered, very well dressed.
Yes.
It runs in the family.
